summary: The note describes the nostril, the external opening of the nose, and its role in moving air and other gases into the nasal cavities. It covers differences across animals, including turbinates in birds and mammals, the single nostril of Cyclostomi, and fish smelling holes. It also covers human nasal anatomy and the nasal cycle, nasal hair filtering, nostril-based smell perception, and the evolutionary migration of excurrent nostrils shown by the fossil Kenichthys campbelli.
one_line: Overview of the nostril, the nasal opening that moves air and gases, with comparative anatomy across animals and human nasal features.
key_facts: A nostril (or naris) is either of the two orifices of the nose that enable the entry and exit of air and other gasses through the nasal cavities.
In birds and mammals, nasal turbinates warm air on inhalation and remove moisture on exhalation.
Fish do not breathe through noses but have two small holes used for smelling, which can also be called nostrils.
Cyclostomi are the exception among fish in having just one nostril.
In humans, the nasal cycle is the normal ultradian cycle of each nostril's blood vessels becoming engorged in swelling, then shrinking.
The nostrils are separated by the septum, which can sometimes be deviated, causing one nostril to appear larger than the other.
Like other tetrapods, humans have two external nostrils (anterior nares) and two posterior nostrils (choanae) at the back of the nasal cavity.
The nasopharynx connects the nose to the throat, aiding in respiration.
The fossilized fish Kenichthys campbelli, 395 million years old, has two nostrils between its front teeth, showing the migration of excurrent nostrils into the mouth.
Two nostrils between the front teeth are similar to human embryos at an early stage; if they fail to join up, the result is a cleft palate.
Each external nostril contains approximately 1,000 strands of nasal hair, which filter foreign particles such as pollen and dust.
Humans can smell different olfactory inputs in the two nostrils and experience a perceptual rivalry akin to binocular rivalry.
Scent information from the two nostrils produces two types of neural activity, with the first cycle corresponding to the ipsilateral and the second to the contralateral odor representations.
The Procellariiformes are distinguished from other birds by having tubular extensions of their nostrils.
Widely-spaced nostrils, like those of the hammerhead shark, may be useful in determining the direction of an odour's source.
